attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you brainstorm the functions that might be added to set up each screen in the tower defense project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

N/A 


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the structure of Red Belt Build activities differ from previous belts in IMPACT?

❓ What functions might be used to set up the 3 levels and multiple waves, throughout the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the structure of Red Belt will differ from prior belts in IMPACT. In Red Belt, multiple Build activities across the level will be used to construct a larger, complex project based on a given theme (instead of multiple, individual projects). The starter code for each successive Build activity will be populated with code from the previous Build activity. At the end of the level, the ninja will have an opportunity to create their own complex project to add to their Red Belt portfolio, using theme-specific concepts applied throughout the Build activities.

💡 If a ninja is unfamiliar with a tower defense style of game, guide them through the basic features. The user will set up towers throughout the game area. Once towers have been placed, the wave will begin where enemies will move across the screen. The towers will send projectiles towards the enemies. The user’s score increases for each enemy destroyed, but decreases if there are enemies that are able to progress through the path at the end of each wave. Each wave gets progressively faster and more challenging as more enemies appear on screen.

💡 Prompt the ninja to brainstorm specific functions that might be needed to set up each screen in the tower defense project. Encourage the ninja to write down ideas as pseudocode to think through the sequence and the logic of the tower defense code.
steps.instructions:
This is the fourth of 4 Build activities where you will create a tower defense project!


Notice that the code from the Build 3 activity has already been added into the JavaScript editor.


In the fourth Build activity, you will finalize the UI/UX features of the project by designing splash screens and opening and closing project sequences. You’ll also update the level select screen, to provide the user with a better sense of the level options to select from.


What functions might be used to set up each screen in the tower defense project?

steps.hints: ❓Did you delete the existing code inside the callScene function that ran when sceneNum equaled 0 or 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might the code inside the callScene function that runs if sceneNum equals 0 or 1 be deleted?

❓ What might happen when the callSplash function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The code currently inside the callScene function that runs if sceneNum equals 0 or 1 is placeholder start and Level Select screen code. This allowed the ninja to test out the start sequence functionality and ensure that each level’s tilemap worked correctly. In this activity, the ninja will use descriptive assets to enhance the Start and Level Select screens of the project.
steps.instructions:
Improve the user experience by customizing the splash screen! 


First, add a Splash sprite kind. Then, under // game functions, define a callSplash function. 


Inside the callScene function definition, delete all of the code that is called if sceneNum equals 0 or 1.  Then, call the callSplash function when sceneNum equals 0.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the existing assets from the Assets tab to add a background, text, and animated sprites to the splash screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What might be updated in the background, title, and Splash sprite animation assets?

❓ Where might the Splash sprites be placed on the Start screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Even though the assets are provided for the Start screen background, title, and Splash sprites, encourage the ninja to customize them to add their own ideas! Prompt the ninja to tinker with the color of the text, the position of the Splash sprites, and even the animation assets to customize the appearance of the Start screen.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the callSplash code, then tinker with the position of the Splash sprites to create a clean Start screen that will grab the user’s attention.
steps.instructions:
Create a customized splash screen to display at the beginning of the game!


Inside the callSplash function definition, add the following code comments, which will organize the code for each part of the Splash screen: // background and title, // turtle animation, // crab animation.


Set the background image to the splashBackground image asset, then add the game title by using the splashText image asset to create a Splash sprite.


Create additional Splash sprites using both the splashTurtleImage and splashCrabImage assets, then set their position to either side of the title and add code to run their respective animations.  


Click ▶ to see the splash screen elements appear, then use the paint editor to edit or replace the different elements and tinker with the code until everything looks as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you leave the background image on screen so the Level Select menu images can appear on top of it?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How can you access the pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function?

❓ Where can you access the names of the 3 levelSelect image assets?

❓ Where might the 4 text sprites be placed on screen so that they align with the levelSelect image assets?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed is a “secret menu” function that can only be accessed via the code completion tool. The ninja should type the menu category controller followed by a dot operator, then select the function name from the code completion tool and type a pair of parentheses to call the function, like this:

controller.pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed()

💡 Prompt the ninja to open My Assets to identify the names of each levelSelect image asset to use in the code.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the callMenu and callSplash code, then tinker with the position of the text sprites to create a clean Level Select screen that will provide the user with information about what path to select.
steps.instructions:
Create and display a customized Level Select screen.


Inside the callScene function definition if sceneNum equals 0, after the callSplash() function call, use the pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function to wait until the user presses any button to move on to the Level Select screen. Then, destroy all Splash sprites and call callScene(1).


Under // game functions, define a callMenu function. Inside the function definition, create 3 Splash sprites that will display the 3 levelSelect image assets on screen. Notice that each levelSelect image contains a small version of the tilemap placed on a transparent background that is the size of the simulator and will not need its position set.



Call the callMenu function inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum equals 1 to see all 3 levelSelect sprites on screen.


Then, use 4 createTextSprite functions to add text that invites the user to “Choose a path!” and then identifies the paths as “Easy”, “Medium”, or “Hard”.


Click ▶ to test the transition from the Start screen to the Level Select screen, then tinker with the code until everything looks as expected

steps.hints: ❓Did you add code to destroy all Splash, ScreenText, and Cursor sprites inside all 3 of the conditional statements, so the sprites are not destroyed before the level is called?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the code need to check if the Cursor overlaps with a Splash sprite, the A button is pressed, and the Splash sprite’s image equals 1 of the 3 image assets used to create the Level Select screen at once?

❓ Does the corresponding level load when the Easy, Medium, and Hard levels are chosen on the Level Select screen?

❓ Which function variable should be used to access the Splash sprite in the overlapsWith functions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider the sequence of the conditional statements inside the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval code. The redundant code is necessary because all 3 conditions need to be checked at the same time in all instances. If the code checked if only the Cursor is overlapping with a Splash sprite and if the A button is pressed before checking for the Splash sprite’s image, it would always lead to the easy level tilemap being displayed.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the callScene code thoroughly, ensuring that their code sequence is correct and that the corresponding tilemap level loads when chosen from the Level Select screen.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the sprite function variable to access the Splash sprite being overlapped in each overlapsWith functions.
steps.instructions:
Code the Level Select screen functionality.


Inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum equals 1, use the createCursor function to create an arrow cursor on screen. 


From Sprite Utils, drag [run code on (sprite) of (kind) update every (500) ms] underneath, setting the kind to Splash and the interval to 100. 


Inside, add a if conditionals that checks for these 2 things to be true: the Cursor overlaps with a Splash sprite and the A button is pressed. Inside the conditional statement, destroy all Splash, ScreenText, and Cursor sprites to clear the screen.


Add 3 nested if conditionals that check if the Splash sprite’s image equals 1 of the 3 image assets used to create the Level Select screen, then use the callScene function, passing the respective sceneNum argument to call the correct level tilemap to load.


Click ▶ to test the Level Select screen functionality for all 3 levels.

steps.hints: ❓Did you place the printDialog functions inside the correct part of the callScene function definition so they appear after the user has pressed a button to clear the splash screen sprites but before the Level Select screen elements appear?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What information would be helpful for the user to know before they begin the Tower Defense project?

❓ Where should the directions be positioned so that they are clearly visible on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Brainstorm with the ninja what information to include in the project directions. What is the user’s goal in the Tower Defense project? What buttons are needed to successfully play the game? What other context is needed to help the user win the game? When does the game end?
steps.instructions:
Add on-screen project instructions.


Inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum equals 0, use multiple printDialog functions from Story to display game instructions for the user after they have pressed any button to start before callScene(1) runs. 


Consider what information is important to share with the user here, including the goal of the game and which buttons to use to open the Inventory menu and place a Tower on the tilemap.


Click ▶ to see the game instructions appear on screen, on top of the existing background image. Tinker with the parameters to adjust the position and color of the text and textbox.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the unloadTilemap function to remove the tilemap before displaying the background image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the unloadTilemap function do? How is it being used to display the Game Over screen?

❓ What will happen when the callScene function is called if sceneNum equals 5?

❓ Does the gameOverText image asset appear when callScene(5) runs?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The unloadTilemap function unloads the current tilemap so that there is no tilemap currently active. This function removes the current tilemap from the screen, so that the background image can be displayed without the tilemap interfering with it. 

💡 When the callScene(5) is called, the gameWave and levelStarted variables will be set to false to remove the user’s button functionality, all Enemy, Tower, PathEnd, Cursor, Projectile, and ScreenText sprites will be destroyed, and the gameOverText image asset will be displayed on screen, signaling the end of the game.
steps.instructions:
Create a Game Over screen!


Inside the callScene function definition, add another conditional that checks if sceneNum equals 5, which will be used to display a Game Over screen when the final game wave ends or the lives count reaches 0. Add a // game over screen comment inside the conditional. 


Inside the conditional, set both the gameWave and levelStarted variables to false, then destroy all Enemy, Tower, PathEnd, Cursor, Projectile, and ScreenText sprites.


From Tile Util, drag [unload current tilemap] underneath to remove the current tilemap from screen. Then, use the splashBackground image asset to set the background image, and create a Splash sprite using the gameOverText image asset.


Under // run game, update the argument passed to the callScene function to 5 to test the Game Over screen.


Click ▶ to see the Game Over screen, then tinker with the code until everything looks as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you place all of the code from this step in the after function, otherwise it might run before it should.
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the text sprite be placed so that it appears below the gameOverText image asset?

❓ Is the user directed back to the Level Select screen when any button is pressed after 2 seconds have passed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the callScene(5) code thoroughly, ensuring that their code sequence is correct and that the Level Select screen loads when any button is pressed after 2 seconds have passed.
steps.instructions:
Provide the user with the option to play again!


Add the timers extension to the project. Use the after function to wait 2 seconds before text on screen prompts the user to press any key to play again. 


Use the createTextSprite function to create the text, and the pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function to wait until the user presses a button to continue. Then, destroy all Splash and ScreenText sprites, and use callScene(1) to skip the Start screen and game instructions and go directly to the Level Select screen.


Click ▶ to test the Game Over screen functionality, ensuring the game restart works as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you check the sequence of your code to ensure the conditional that codes the sounds and screen effects runs at the correct time?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition ends the game in a win? What condition ends the game in a loss?

❓ What sounds and screen effects might play when the user wins the game? When they lose the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use Ctrl + F to search for the gameOver function name in the code to easily edit each instance.

💡 Prompt the ninja to identify the winning and losing conditions of the game, in order to populate the conditional code. The game will end in a loss if the lives count reaches 0. Else, it will end in a win once the final game wave ends.
steps.instructions:
Code the conditions that trigger the Game Over screen to load.


In the Enemy/endTile onOverlapTile function and the endWave function definition, replace the gameOver functions with callScene(5) to call the customized Game Over screen.  


Inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum equals 5, above the after function, add an if/else conditional that checks if the value of the lives variable is less than zero. Play a sound in the background and start a screen effect that is either positive or negative, based on the game ending in a win or a loss. 


Inside the after function, stop all sounds and end the screen effects after the user has pressed any button.


Under // run game, update the argument passed to the callScene function to 0 to test the Game Over screen.


Click ▶ to test the Game Over screen functionality, ensuring the correct sounds and screen effects run when the game ends in a win or in a loss.

steps.hints: ❓Did you check the position of the stopAllSounds functions to ensure they stop the music where expected, and do not unexpectedly prevent other sounds from playing?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What functions and parameters are needed to play the waveSong asset? 

❓ When does the waveSong asset play throughout the project? 

❓ What might be updated in the waveSong asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the code documentation tool to guide them in adding arguments to pass to the music.play function. Notice where they have left out needed parentheses or symbols to ensure the waveSong asset loops in the background of the project.

💡 The waveSong asset will play throughout each wave. The music will stop once the wave has stopped, and will start again once the next wave begins. It will also stop when the Game over screen is displayed at the end of the project. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to tinker with the waveSong asset in the music editor. Prompt the ninja to tinker with the notes and bring their own song creations to life! 

💡 Adding background music to a project enhances the User Experience of a project by making it multi-sensory. It also signals when certain actions are happening (e.g. that the wave is running), providing additional information throughout a project.
steps.instructions:
Add background music that plays during a game wave.


Inside the startWave function definition, use the play function with music.createSong as the first argument to play the waveSong asset, looping in the background, when a game wave begins. 


Then, in the endWave function definition and in the callScene function definition when sceneNum equals 5, use the stopAllSounds function to stop the music from looping in the background at the end of the game wave and when the Game Over screen appears.


Under // run game, update the argument passed to the callScene function to 2, 3, or 4 to test the game wave music. Open the waveSong asset in the Music Editor to tinker with the song asset, or create an original song to use for the game wave.


Click ▶ to test the game wave song functionality.

steps.hints: ❓Did you make additional updates to the project’s assets or code to further improve the User Experience (UX)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What else could be added or modified to further improve and customize this project?

❓ What is something you used to create this project that could be applied to your Adventure project?

❓ What other strategies might you use to debug an error in the code with a project of this size?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Once the ninja has completed the project, invite them to debrief about the process. What did they feel confident in? Which parts were hard? What else might they change about the process? Encourage the ninja to reflect on the size of this project, emphasizing that it required 4 Build activities to create. With this in mind, they will create an Adventure project of a similar size and complexity to demonstrate the concepts that they’ve learned during this level. Prompt the ninja to identify 2-3 things that they used to create the Tower Defense project that they plan to incorporate into their Adventure project.

💡 Encourage the ninja to playtest their project with other ninjas as well. Provide sentence starters to the ninjas to encourage both positive and constructive feedback, then work with the ninja to identify pieces of feedback to incorporate into their code.

💡 One useful debugging strategy for large projects is to use the sayText function, especially to check that variables and arrays are updating correctly throughout the project. Review the ninja’s code together, looking for areas that could be improved, then insert the sayText function to test the source of the issue.
steps.instructions:
Playtest, debug, and refactor the project!


This project took 4 different Build activities to complete and there are a lot of moving pieces within it! 


Under // run game, update the argument passed to the callScene function to 0 to be able to playtest the project from the beginning. 


Play the project several times and think about what’s working well and what could be improved. Show the project to another ninja or Code Sensei for additional feedback. Make any necessary updates to further improve the User Experience (UX) of the game.


During playtesting, try to identify any actions that seem to work sometimes, but aren’t always consistent. Review the code in the editor to debug what the issue might be. Don’t forget to comment out code or use the sayText function to “say” the value of a variable, to test a small chunk of code at a time.


Click ▶ to test and improve the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Complete the Tower Defense project by designing the start, level select, and game over screens!

validationItems.text: Use a function to create then call a customized splash screen as the game start screen.
Add on-screen game directions that appear after the game start screen.
Use a function to create then call a level select screen that appears after the game directions.
Create a Game Over screen with different sounds / effects that happen based on a win or a lose condition. Use on-screen text to prompt the user to play again.
Add background music that plays during a game wave.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Red Belt! In this level, you’ll apply your previous learning by creating a complex tower defense project in JavaScript across 4 different Build activities. There is no pre-assessment Quest activity for this level, so click “Start Level” to begin! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2

badges.title: Tower Power!
badges.description: Create a complex tower defense project in JavaScript using sprite and tile utility extensions, and a detailed Inventory menu.
